items.title: The oxygen you breathe comes from WATER, not CO2
items.claim: Photosynthesis takes in CO2 and water and produces sugar and oxygen. Every chemistry student writes the equation. But the O2 released is not stripped from the CO2 — it comes entirely from splitting water molecules.
items.prompt: How do we know the oxygen comes from water?

options.text: Both water and CO2 contribute oxygen equally
Ruben and Kamen (1941) used the heavy isotope oxygen-18 to label either water or CO2; the released O2 carried the label only when the water was labelled, never when the CO2 was
CO2 is the source of the oxygen

items.reveal:
The light reactions of photosynthesis split water (photolysis) at the oxygen-evolving complex — a manganese-calcium cluster in Photosystem II. Two water molecules are split: 2 H2O -> 4 H+ + 4 e- + O2.

The electrons enter the electron transport chain. The protons contribute to the thylakoid pH gradient (lumen reaches pH ~5, stroma ~8). ATP synthase uses the gradient to make ATP.

The Calvin cycle (in the stroma) uses ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into sugar. The carbon from CO2 becomes the carbon in glucose. But the oxygen atoms in CO2 mostly end up in carbohydrate, NOT in the released O2.

Oxygen is, from photosynthesis's point of view, a waste product — and arguably the most consequential pollution event in Earth's history (the Great Oxidation Event, ~2.4 billion years ago, killed most anaerobic life).
items.why: The arrow-pushing equation suggests CO2 donates oxygen. The actual chemistry inverts that: water is split, CO2 is reduced, and the oxygen you breathe was once dissolved in a chloroplast.

items.title: The avocado was made for a giant ground sloth
items.claim: Avocado fruit has a huge stone surrounded by lipid-rich flesh. No living mammal can swallow it whole. The fruit's design anticipated a disperser — likely the now-extinct Pleistocene megafauna (giant ground sloths, gomphotheres). The plant outlived its partner.
items.prompt: What does this tell us about coevolution?

options.text: Plants and dispersers shape each other's traits over millions of years; when the partner goes extinct, the plant may persist with traits that look maladaptive in the present — ecological 'ghosts of evolution past'
Plants don't need animals for dispersal
Coevolved plants always go extinct with their partners

items.reveal:
Daniel Janzen and Paul Martin (1982) proposed the concept of 'anachronistic fruits': fruits whose size, hardness, smell or chemistry seem designed for dispersers that no longer exist.

North American megafauna went extinct ~13,000 years ago (climate change plus human hunting): mastodons, giant ground sloths (up to 6 metres tall), gomphotheres, glyptodonts. Many large-fruited Central American trees — avocados, papayas, large legume pods — appear to have coevolved with these animals.

Without megafaunal dispersal, these trees rely on humans, water, or rare alternatives (jaguars eat avocados; tapirs swallow some seeds whole). Many would have declining ranges if not for human cultivation.

Osage orange (Maclura pomifera): grapefruit-sized fruits with little use to modern animals. Likely a mastodon plant. Now native to a small Texas range; spread widely only because humans use it as windbreaks and hedges.

Coffee, cacao, durian — all probably coevolved with mammalian dispersers and rely on living relatives or human cultivation for survival.

The broader point: present-day ecology contains relics from past ecologies. Some traits make sense only in the context of vanished species and lost interactions.
items.why: Coevolution implies tight mutual adaptation. When one partner disappears, the other can persist but appears strangely engineered for a world that no longer exists.

items.title: Plants and oceans cycle far more CO2 than humans release — yet we still drive the trend
items.claim: Humans emit ~10 gigatonnes of carbon per year. Natural fluxes (photosynthesis ~120 Gt, ocean exchange ~80 Gt, respiration ~120 Gt) dwarf this. Yet atmospheric CO2 keeps rising. The natural fluxes are roughly balanced — human emissions are a small but unmatched addition.
items.prompt: Why does a small flux dominate the trend?

options.text: The large natural fluxes are bidirectional and roughly balanced; the small human flux is NET addition. Imagine a bath whose inflow exactly equals outflow — a slow added trickle raises the water level whether the main flow is large or not
Plants absorb only certain types of CO2

items.reveal_title: Flux vs reservoir vs net change
items.reveal:
Reservoirs (rough sizes in gigatonnes of carbon):
Atmosphere: ~880 (and rising)
Oceans: ~38,000 (most as dissolved bicarbonate, slow exchange with deep ocean)
Soils: ~1,500-2,400
Vegetation: ~450-650
Fossil fuels: ~4,000+ (decreasing as we burn them)

Fluxes (Gt C per year):
Photosynthesis: ~120 (atmosphere to land)
Land respiration: ~120 (back to atmosphere)
Ocean uptake: ~80 (atmosphere to ocean)
Ocean release: ~78 (ocean to atmosphere)
Fossil emissions: ~10 (geological store to atmosphere)
Land-use change: ~1-2 net (mostly deforestation)

The natural fluxes are within ~1% of balance. The fossil flux is unbalanced — it's NET addition with no matching natural removal at the same scale. About half is absorbed by oceans and land 'sinks'; half stays airborne. Atmospheric CO2 rises ~2.5 ppm/year.

Residence time vs adjustment time: an individual CO2 molecule exchanges with the ocean in years. But removing the EXCESS takes much longer (hundreds to thousands of years for the surface ocean, ~100,000 years for full geological recovery).
items.why: The 'humans only emit 4% of CO2 turnover' argument confuses flux with net change. A small net addition into a near-balanced cycle is what matters, and it accumulates.
